title: Experimental and Non-Experimental Research Designs
summary: Pre-experimental designs; true-experimental designs; pretest-post-test; Solomon four-group; Latin square; participant design; quasi-experimental; non-equivalent groups; longitudinal; time-series; regression discontinuity; cross-sectional; cohort sequential; ex-post facto.
objectives: Classify designs as pre-experimental, true-experimental or quasi-experimental.
Explain random assignment as the distinguishing feature.
Describe Solomon four-group and Latin square designs.
revision: True-experimental needs random assignment. Solomon four-group controls pretest sensitisation. Quasi lacks randomisation.
confusions: Believing Latin square controls for all confounds.

i: One-shot case study — single group, one treatment, one observation.
One-group pretest-posttest — one group tested before and after treatment.
Static group comparison — two groups, one treated, compared after treatment.

r: Random assignment; pretest and posttest for both groups.
Four groups; controls for pretest sensitisation.
Controls for order and sequence effects.

i: Non-equivalent groups design — no random assignment.
Cross-sectional — different participants at one time.
Cohort sequential — combines longitudinal and cross-sectional.
Ex-post facto — studies events after they occurred.

notes.t: The Solomon four-group design controls for pretest sensitisation by including groups with and without pretest, crossed with treatment and control. It is the strongest true-experimental design for isolating treatment effects.
Random assignment distinguishes true-experimental from quasi-experimental designs. Solomon four-group controls pretest sensitisation. Frequently tested distinctions.

OCR-extracted from source page 235: Research designs are classified into three major categories: Pre-Experimental, True-Experimental and Quasi-Experimental. True-experimental designs require random assignment; quasi-experimental designs do not.
